payload.name: Enumeration search for which-achievement questions
payload.description: When a question asks which achievements, records, career-highs, or performances someone achieved, treat it as an exhaustive enumeration and search each possible subcategory.
content: When a question asks 'Which <achievement-type> did <entity> achieve?' (e.g., which career-high performances, records, awards, milestones), treat it as an enumeration request whose answer may span multiple distinct items in separate memories.

Do not finalize an answer after the first retrieved item; run additional searches using terms for each plausible subcategory of the achievement type (e.g., for career-high performances: points, assists, rebounds, blocks; for awards: specific award names) and synonyms for 'highest'/'best'.

Check sufficiency after each search: if new searches return distinct items, continue; only answer when additional searches yield no new items, and include all retrieved memories that match the asked category.

candidates.solves: The access agent answered an enumerative 'which achievements/performances' question after retrieving only one of two expected career-high items, because it treated the question as a single-item lookup. Reusable guidance is to treat such 'which' questions as exhaustive enumeration requests across subcategories, and to keep searching until no new items appear. This applies to any future question asking which records, awards, or best performances someone achieved, independent of the specific domain.

payload.name: SearchRelatedActivitiesForWritingKinds
payload.description: When a question asks what kind of writing someone does or produces, and initial searches return only explicit writing projects, run additional searches for writing-adjacent activities (forum participation, discussions, comments, recommendations) before answering.
content: When a question asks what kinds of writing a person does, do not treat a search that returns explicit writing projects (articles, novels, stories) as sufficient; also run supplementary searches using related-activity terms such as '<person> forum', '<person> discussion', '<person> comments', '<person> recommendations', and '<person> sharing'.

When judging evidence sufficiency for such questions, treat event memories that describe writing-adjacent activities (e.g., participating in a forum, discussing books, making recommendations) as evidence of writing, even when they do not use the word 'write' or 'writing'.

candidates.solves: Questions that enumerate a person's types of writing are often answered incompletely because retrieval targets the literal word 'writing' and misses memories describing writing-adjacent activities like forum discussions, comments, or recommendations. This adds supplementary searches for those related activities and clarifies that such memories count as evidence, preventing partial answers in future equivalent queries.

payload.name: Count creative works via synonym and completion terms
payload.description: When a question asks how many creative works (screenplays, books, scripts, films) a person has written or completed, expand retrieval with synonyms and ordinal/completion wording.
content: For count questions about written/completed creative works, search not only the exact artifact word (e.g., screenplay) but also synonyms (script, story, project) and ordinal/completion phrases (second, third, finished, completed) that may identify additional instances.
Inspect event and plan memories for completion or achievement predicates even if they do not use the exact artifact noun; treat distinct completed works as separate counted items.
Continue alternate-term searches until no new distinct work appears before answering the count.

candidates.solves: Count questions about written/creative works often miss instances when retrieval only uses exact artifact noun (screenplay) but a supporting memory uses synonyms (script) or ordinals (second). Future count queries should expand vocabulary to capture all distinct works before answering.

payload.name: Pre-event problem search via seek/criteria terms
payload.description: When a question asks about problems, challenges, or difficulties faced before a specific event, supplement problem-synonym searches with the person's stated search criteria or desires.
content: If a question asks about problems, challenges, or difficulties a person faced before a specific event or in a given area, do not search only with negative/problem vocabulary. Also run searches for the person's stated search criteria or desires using phrases like '<person> looking for', '<person> seeking', '<person> wanted/needed', '<person> hoping to find' together with the relevant area (e.g., housing, pet, job, school).

When judging evidence sufficiency for such questions, treat memories that describe an active search with concrete requirements or constraints (e.g., 'looking for a smaller breed suitable for apartments', 'seeking a neighborhood near parks') as valid evidence of pre-event problems, even if they never explicitly use the word 'problem' or 'challenge'.

candidates.solves: When a question asks about problems before a milestone event, retrieval may miss memories describing the pre-event search in neutral terms (looking for, seeking). Search with the person's stated criteria or requirements so implied obstacles become retrievable. Applies when a pre-event difficulty query returns no evidence but an active search with constraints exists.

payload.name: EnumerateDistinctItemsForPluralQueries
payload.description: When a query asks for a list of a person's classes, courses, activities, or similar items (e.g., 'what classes did X take'), search with varied synonyms and include event/plan memories, then answer with all distinct items found.
content: If a question asks for a plural set of a person's items (e.g., classes, courses, hobbies, goals, activities), treat it as an enumeration query: do not stop after finding one supporting memory.

Run additional searches with synonyms and related terms (e.g., class, course, workshop, training, seminar, program) and do not restrict memory_kinds; include event and plan memories, since signed-up or upcoming activities are often stored there.
After retrieval, compile every distinct concrete item mentioned across the supporting memories and answer with the full list, not just the first or most prominent result.

candidates.solves: The agent answered a plural enumeration question (e.g., 'what classes did X take') with only one retrieved course, despite other memories mentioning additional classes/workshops stored under different terms (workshop, course) and in event/plan memories. The abstract failure is premature convergence on a single search result and insufficient query variation for list questions. This skill applies to any future question asking for multiple distinct items a person has, took, signed up for, or participates in, where complete enumeration requires synonym expansion and broad memory-kind retrieval.

payload.name: EnumerateProducedWorkCategories
payload.description: When a question asks what kind(s) of something a person produces or does (e.g., writings, music, art), search for all distinct categories including past and one-off works, not only current projects.
content: For questions asking the kind(s)/type(s) of work a person produces (writings, music, art, etc.), do not limit retrieval to current/ongoing projects; treat the question as an enumeration of all distinct categories.
Use query expansions with concrete subtype terms (e.g., 'blog post', 'journal', 'book', 'screenplay', 'poem') plus the generic category, and search memory_kinds 'event', 'profile', and 'state'.

If initial results contain only current projects, run additional searches for past works and indirect mentions (e.g., letters, reviews, responses) using predicates like 'writes', 'creates', 'publishes', or 'impact'.
Before answering, check whether the retrieved memories collectively represent multiple distinct categories; if not, search again with broader or alternative subtype terms.

candidates.solves: The agent answered only from current projects because the selected skill focused on ongoing creative work, missing past and indirect writing evidence such as a produced screenplay and a blog post described through a reader's letter. The rule generalizes to any question that asks for the set of categories of something a person produces, requiring exhaustive retrieval across time and subtypes. This applies to future queries like 'What kinds of music does X make?' or 'What types of art does X create?'.

payload.name: completed-activity-evidence-rule
payload.description: When a question asks what activities a person has done, tried, or participated in, use only explicit participation evidence, exclude interests/plans, and search exhaustively for all completed activities before answering.
content: When a question asks what activities a person has done, tried, or participated in (e.g., 'has done', 'has tried', 'has participated in'), treat only statements that explicitly describe the person actually performing/participating in the activity as evidence. Do not treat expressions of interest, desire, preference, or future plans as evidence of having done it.

Before finalizing an answer to such a completed-activity question, run multiple varied searches (including participation phrasing and concrete candidate activity names) to discover all distinct completed activities; include only activities with explicit participation evidence and note that mere interest does not count.

candidates.solves: The agent answered 'what activities has X done' by including activities the person only expressed interest in, and stopped after one concrete activity without searching for additional completed ones. This rule supplies the missing decision boundary: for any future completed-activity enumeration question, require explicit past-participation evidence and run varied searches before finalizing. It does not apply to 'enjoys', 'interested in', or 'plans to' questions, which legitimately use preference/plan memories.

payload.name: Broken-Item Synonym-Expanded Searches
payload.description: When a question asks what things a person or entity had broken, damaged, or not working, use this to expand retrieval beyond the literal word 'broken'.
content: When a question asks what things a person/entity had broken, damaged, or not working, do not rely solely on the literal term 'broken'; run additional keyword/hybrid searches using paraphrases such as 'broke down', 'malfunctioned', 'had an accident', 'needs repair', 'out of order', 'issue with', combined with the subject and plausible item categories (e.g., vehicle, car, appliance, device).

If the initial retrieval returns memories about activities involving an item (e.g., a road trip or accident) but none explicitly say 'broken', run follow-up searches for that item plus failure/repair vocabulary (e.g., 'accident', 'breakdown', 'repair shop') before deciding there is no information.

Treat 'What kinds of things did <entity> have broken?' as an enumeration request: check sufficiency after each search and continue until no new distinct broken/damaged items appear; do not finalize a 'no information' answer after a single top-k retrieval.

candidates.solves: When a user asks what things a person had broken or damaged, the initial literal search often misses memories that use verbs like 'broke down', 'malfunctioned', or 'had an accident'. In this diagnosis the agent searched once with 'broken', retrieved only unrelated events, and answered 'no information' even though a supporting memory described a vehicle breakdown. Future questions of the same enumerative type need a synonym-expansion step before concluding no evidence, using failure/repair vocabulary and relevant item categories.

payload.name: Expand abstract strategy questions with concrete plan terms
payload.description: When a question asks what strategy, advice, or method people discussed, suggested, or recommended (e.g., for studying, time management), also search with concrete implementation terms and include plan-kind memories.
content: If a user asks what strategy, technique, or advice someone discussed, suggested, or recommended, do not rely only on the abstract query phrasing; run supplementary keyword searches with concrete terms likely stored in memories, such as 'study plan', 'planners', 'schedulers', 'breaking tasks', 'setting goals', and include plan-kind memories.

When judging evidence sufficiency for such questions, treat a plan memory recording an offer or suggestion by one person to another as direct evidence of the discussed strategy, even if it does not use the word 'strategy' or the exact topic wording.

candidates.solves: The Access Agent failed to retrieve a plan memory that directly recorded the discussed study/time-management suggestion because its queries used abstract terms ('helpful strategy', 'time management') while the memory stored concrete implementation terms ('study plan', 'planners or schedulers', 'breaking tasks'). This recurs whenever a question asks about discussed advice or strategies and memories record the advice as concrete plans or suggestions. Supplementary searches with concrete terms and inclusion of plan-kind memories make the retrieval generalize across such topics.

payload.name: Structured retrieval on project predicate
payload.description: When a question asks about a person's projects, plans, or what they are working on, run a structured search filtering event memories with predicate 'project' in addition to any free-text hybrid search.
content: When the question asks about someone's projects, future plans, or current work, run a structured search with memory_kind='event' and predicate='project' (optionally filtered by the person's subject) in addition to any hybrid/free-text search.

Do not require project memories to contain the literal words 'project' or 'plan' in their text; the predicate 'project' is the reliable signal, and stated interests or intentions (e.g., 'interested in', 'aims to', 'wants to') may be stored as event memories with past or unspecified dates while still representing future plans.
Before answering, combine evidence from the predicate-filtered event retrieval with any retrieved plan memories, and judge sufficiency against all current related memories.

candidates.solves: When a question asks what projects a person is planning, working on, or intends to do, free-text hybrid search can miss event memories that carry the predicate 'project' but do not contain the literal words 'project' or 'plan'. This skill adds a structured retrieval on the 'project' predicate so such stated interests and intentions are surfaced for evidence. It applies to any future project-oriented question about any person.

payload.name: Evaluative period retrieval with polarity and domain terms
payload.description: When a question asks whether a time period was good, bad, successful, or difficult for someone's career or work, search for both positive and negative outcome events using domain-specific vocabulary before concluding.
content: When a question asks whether a time period was good, bad, successful, difficult, or similar for someone's career or work, search for both positive and negative outcome events in that range, not only milestone or success terms.

If the question names a domain (career, school, hobby, etc.), include domain-specific vocabulary beyond the generic label—competition outcomes, project progress, tools/equipment, health, finances—and treat events that clearly affect the person's work as relevant even when they do not contain the domain word.

Before answering an evaluative period question, inspect all retrieved events in the date range; if none support a negative or positive judgment though the question implies one, run additional searches with setback, failure, loss, or incident terms for each subject before concluding no evidence exists.

candidates.solves: The agent searched a date range using only generic career and milestone terms, so it missed setback and work-loss memories stored under domain-specific vocabulary and answered an evaluative period question with no supporting evidence. This skill applies to any question asking whether a time period was good, bad, successful, or difficult for someone's career or work: retrieve both positive and negative outcome events using domain-specific vocabulary, and do not stop after generic searches. It does not apply to plain factual date or count questions that do not ask for a polarity judgment.

payload.name: ExpandSearchForEnumeratedKindsOfWork
payload.description: When a question asks what kinds or types of projects, works, or items someone has, run additional searches for concrete named instances before answering.
content: When the question asks what kinds/types of a person's projects, works, or items, do not stop after a single query using only the category label; run at least one additional search with concrete object terms and predicate verbs (e.g., designed, built, developed, prototype, accomplishment).
Include event memories with predicates like 'project' or 'accomplishment' even if they lack the category word from the question.
If only generic memories are returned, search again with alternative terms and enumerate all distinct named instances before answering.

candidates.solves: The agent answered with generic memories because the query used only the category label and missed specific named projects stored without that label. This lexical mismatch affects any question enumerating kinds of a person's projects, works, or possessions. The rule adds searches with concrete object and predicate terms so all distinct instances are recovered before answering.

payload.name: Expand project queries with intention and goal terms
payload.description: When a question asks about a person's projects, plans, goals, or future intentions, expand retrieval with intention/interest verbs (interested in, aims to, wants to, hopes to) and goal nouns (goals, ambitions), and include event memories with predicate 'project'.
content: When a question asks about someone's projects, plans, goals, or what they want to do, expand the query with intention and interest verbs such as 'interested in', 'aims to', 'wants to', 'hopes to', 'plans to', plus goal-related terms like 'goals', 'ambitions', 'future work'. Relevant memories may state the intention without using the literal words 'project' or 'plan'.

For such questions, search event memories with predicate 'project' even if the memory text lacks the word 'project' or 'plan'; judge relevance by the stated intention/interest, not by exact keyword overlap.
If initial results return only current activities or leisure plans, rerun with expansions centered on the person's goals and values before answering 'no information'.

candidates.solves: Retrieval for questions about a person's projects, plans, or future intentions often misses relevant memories when those memories use interest/goal phrasing (e.g., 'interested in', 'aims to') instead of the literal words 'project' or 'plan'. This rule instructs the access agent to expand queries with intention and goal vocabulary and to include event memories with predicate 'project' regardless of surface wording, so it applies to any future question about someone's planned work or goals where the supporting memory is an enriched intent event.

payload.name: Search concrete activities for career development questions
payload.description: When a question asks what professional activities, career-building steps, or experience-gaining activities a person participates in; run searches with concrete activity types and event/achievement phrasings, not only 'experience' meta-labels.
content: When a question asks what professional activities a person participates in to gain experience or build their career, do not rely only on queries containing 'professional', 'experience', or 'career'. Run at least one additional search using concrete activity frames: '[subject] presented at [conference]', '[subject] attends [workshop/training]', '[subject] interns at [firm]', '[subject] volunteers for [organization]', '[subject] is taking [course/certification]'.

Treat event/achievement memories that describe a concrete professional activity (e.g., presenting at a conference, completing a workshop) as directly supporting the answer, even if they do not mention 'experience' or 'professional'.

After retrieving candidate activities, verify the answer covers all professional activities mentioned across event, plan, and state memories; if a candidate activity appears in any memory, search for that concrete activity name before finalizing.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is that all searches reused the meta-labels 'professional activities' and 'experience', so a memory about presenting at a conference was missed. The reusable failure is using abstract career terms instead of concrete activity names when retrieving professional-development activities. The rule applies to questions asking how someone gains experience or builds a career, and it does not apply to hobby/leisure questions already covered by the participation skill.

payload.name: Expand allergy and dietary-restriction searches
payload.description: When a question asks what someone is allergic to or about their dietary restrictions, use this to broaden retrieval beyond literal allergy terms and to verify explicit support.
content: When a question asks about a person's allergies or allergic reactions, expand the search beyond the literal word 'allergy': include terms such as 'intolerant', 'intolerance', 'cannot have', 'cannot eat', 'dairy-free', 'lactose', 'reaction to', and related food/substance restriction vocabulary.

Run an additional retrieval over memories of kind 'preference' and do not restrict memory_kinds to event, because dietary restrictions and intolerances are often stored as preferences rather than as explicit allergy events.

Before finalizing an answer, verify that each listed allergen or restriction is explicitly stated in at least one retrieved memory; if the only support is an implication (e.g., a past reaction to a similar item), exclude it or search again until explicit evidence appears.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause was a single literal 'allergy' search that missed a preference memory about lactose intolerance, and an answer that included an implied allergen without explicit support. The reusable rule is to broaden allergy queries with intolerance/dietary vocabulary, include preference memories, and require explicit evidence for each listed allergen. This applies to any future question about a person's allergies, intolerances, or dietary restrictions.

payload.name: Ailment-cause queries need condition-specific searches
payload.description: When a question asks what ailment, illness, or medical condition a person faces due to a stated cause (e.g., weight, stress, diet), search for named conditions and health events in addition to cause-related terms.
content: When a question asks which ailment/condition is due to a stated cause, do not rely only on a query that combines the cause with generic words like 'ailment' or 'medical condition'; such queries can miss event memories that name the condition but never mention the cause.

After the first search, retrieve the person's health-related memories (e.g., events with health issue predicates, ER visits, doctor warnings) and use the named conditions or visit types from those memories as follow-up search terms.

Also run a supplementary search for the person's health events in the relevant period using terms like '<person> health issue', '<person> ER', or the condition names found, and treat a memory that names the condition as sufficient evidence even if it does not repeat the cause.

candidates.solves: When a question asks which ailment is caused by a stated factor, searching only the factor plus 'ailment' misses memories that name the condition without repeating the factor. The rule is to supplement with condition-specific and health-event searches using terms from health memories. This applies to any cause-to-effect health question expecting a concrete condition rather than a general complaint.

payload.name: Concrete health-incident vocabulary expansion
payload.description: When a question asks what health scares, medical emergencies, or health incidents someone experienced, run additional searches with concrete condition/symptom/event terms instead of only generic health phrases.
content: When a question asks about a person's health scares, medical emergencies, incidents, or wake-up calls, do not rely only on query phrasing like 'health issue' or 'medical problem'. Supporting memories often name the specific condition, symptom, or event (e.g., ER visit, hospitalization, surgery, diagnosis) without using the generic phrase.

Run additional keyword or structured searches combining each named person with concrete medical and incident terms (e.g., pain, diagnosis, ER, hospital, surgery, scare, wake-up call, check-up) and with event verbs like 'experienced', 'suffered', or 'was hospitalized'.

If the question names multiple people or uses a plural like 'scares' or 'incidents', treat it as an enumeration request: after the first retrieval, verify that each named person has at least one distinct incident memory; if not, re-search with alternative concrete terms until all distinct incidents are found.

Do not answer a health-scares question solely from a state memory describing ongoing health struggles or a general check-up; seek event memories that explicitly describe an incident with a specific condition, ER visit, or hospitalization.

candidates.solves: Questions about past health scares or medical incidents fail when retrieval stays on generic phrases like 'health issue' or 'medical problem', while the supporting event memories use concrete condition, symptom, or incident wording and may be split across multiple people or multiple events. This skill applies to factual recall of past health incidents and adds concrete-vocabulary searches plus enumeration/sufficiency checks for multi-person or plural questions; it does not apply to general health-status or health-advice queries.

payload.name: Temporal filtering for visited-place questions
payload.description: When a question asks which places someone visited in a specific month/period, filter candidate location memories by timestamp overlap and do not stop after one out-of-period match.
content: If the question specifies a time period, treat world_start/world_end overlap with that period as a hard filter: do not cite or answer with a location memory whose timestamps fall outside the requested period, even if it matches the person and place names.

When a retrieved travel memory is in-period or uses relative time, resolve its date from the message/session timestamp, then run additional time-filtered searches using that memory's activity/landscape terms (e.g., road trip, skiing, mountains) to find other locations visited in the same period.

If the question asks for places (plural), collect all in-period location memories before answering rather than settling for the first matching place; if an in-period memory names only a city/landmark, infer the containing country and include it.

candidates.solves: Location questions that include a specific month or date range often return travel memories whose timestamps fall outside that range or only a single matching place. The diagnosed failure answered with an off-period place and ignored in-period evidence, so future questions should require temporal filtering of candidate memories and continued time-filtered searching until all in-period locations are collected. This applies to any 'which places did X visit in [period]' question, regardless of entity or country.

payload.name: Enumerate visited cities via event memories
payload.description: When a question asks which cities or places a person has visited, plans to visit, or mentioned visiting, use this Skill to broaden retrieval beyond the literal word 'visit'.
content: When a question asks which cities/places a person has visited or mentioned visiting, do not restrict searches to the phrase 'visited' or to the conversation partner's name. Run supplementary searches combining the person's name with travel/event vocabulary such as 'trip to', 'game in', 'traveled to', 'favorite city', and 'explore'.

Treat a memory as evidence for a city whenever it links the person to that city through any event, plan, or activity (e.g., an event in the city, a planned trip, a location described as a favorite to explore), even if the word 'visit' does not appear.

After collecting candidate cities from event/plan memories, verify each candidate against at least one retrieved memory and answer only from those verified links; do not stop after a single query if the question asks for a list.

candidates.solves: Questions asking which cities/places a person visited or mentioned are missed when retrieval only looks for the verb 'visit' and the conversation partner, while memory stores city links under event/activity predicates (e.g., a game in a city, a trip, a favorite place to explore). The rule broadens search to travel/event vocabulary and accepts any memory linking the person to a city. Applies to any future list-of-cities/places question.

payload.name: PreferCurrentHabitualPlaceOverPastEvent
payload.description: When a question asks where or what type of place someone does a recurring activity (meditates, exercises, studies, reads), do not answer with a one-time past event location before checking for a current habitual place.
content: Before answering a 'where/what type of place does X [activity]' question, treat a retrieved memory that describes a one-time event (e.g., a trip, retreat, or class at a named location) as insufficient by itself if the question implies a recurring practice.

Run at least one supplementary search using habitual/current phrasing, such as '<person> usually/regularly [activity] at' or '<person> goes to ... to [activity]', in addition to the literal question phrasing.

When multiple candidate place memories exist, prefer the one describing an ongoing or repeated practice (present/regular habit) over a past one-time event, and use the memory's world_start and time references to identify which place is current.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: the agent answered a 'where does X [activity]' question using a past one-time event memory, ignoring a memory of the person's current habitual spot. The mechanism is treating any place-related event memory as sufficient for a recurring-practice location question. Future applicability: whenever a question asks for the place where someone regularly performs an activity, search with habitual phrasing and prefer the current recurring location over one-off events.
